title: Reading a run chart
brief:
You are the quality focal person at a district hospital. Your team has been tracking the proportion of mothers initiating breastfeeding within one hour of delivery on the postnatal ward. The chart below shows the last 14 months of weekly data, plotted with a median line.

Before you draw any conclusions, you want to make sure you can read this run chart correctly.

exhibit.title: Early breastfeeding initiation rate (weekly), district hospital

task.stem: Which statement best describes what the dashed line across the middle of this run chart represents?

options.label: The target the team is trying to reach.
The median of all data points on the chart.
The upper control limit (UCL).
The average for the most recent four weeks.

debrief.correct: Yes. The horizontal line on a run chart is the **median** of the data plotted. The median splits the points into halves and is what most run-chart rules (shift, trend, runs) reference. Run charts do **not** have control limits — those belong on Shewhart (control) charts such as p, u, c, or I-MR charts.
debrief.wrong: The horizontal line on a run chart is the **median** of the data plotted — not a target, not a control limit, and not a recent average. The median is the reference for run-chart rules (shift, trend, runs). If you see lines labelled UCL/LCL, you are looking at a control chart, not a run chart.
debrief.rule_cited: Run chart anatomy — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), ch. 4.

title: Find the numerator and denominator
brief:
A clinic in-charge reports their hand-hygiene measure as: **‘Proportion of clinical hand-hygiene moments where staff performed hand hygiene, observed during scheduled audit rounds in the outpatient department in May.’**

A strong measure makes its numerator, denominator, and counting frame unambiguous. Spot the numerator below.

task.stem: Which is the numerator of this measure?

options.label: The number of clinical hand-hygiene moments observed during scheduled audit rounds.
The number of observed moments where staff performed hand hygiene.
The proportion of correct hand-hygiene observations.
The total number of clinical staff working in the outpatient department in May.

debrief.correct: Correct. The **numerator** is the count of events that meet the measure: observed moments where hand hygiene was performed. The **denominator** is the total number of observed clinical hand-hygiene moments. The third option is the resulting proportion (the measure itself), and the fourth is irrelevant to the measure as written.
debrief.wrong: Re-read the measure. The numerator is the count of the events meeting the criterion: ‘moments where staff performed hand hygiene’. The denominator is ‘all clinical hand-hygiene moments observed’. A clear operational definition makes these unambiguous.
debrief.rule_cited: Operational definitions — IHI QI 102 / Provost & Murray ch. 3.

title: Count, classification, or continuous?
brief:
Picking the right chart starts with knowing what kind of data you have. Three categories matter most:

- **Count data** — a count of events in a defined area of opportunity (e.g., number of falls per 1,000 patient-days).
- **Classification data** — each item is sorted into yes/no (e.g., proportion of patients receiving DVT prophylaxis on admission).
- **Continuous data** — measurements on a numeric scale (e.g., length of stay in hours).

Match each measure to its data type.

task.stem: Match each measure to its data type.

items.label: Door-to-needle time for stroke thrombolysis (minutes).
Proportion of post-partum mothers screened for depression before discharge.
Number of needle-stick injuries per month in the laboratory.
Proportion of children under five with a complete vaccination card.

debrief.correct: Well done. Knowing the data structure is the first step in choosing the right chart. Continuous → I-MR (or X-bar & S). Classification → p-chart. Count of events in an area of opportunity → u-chart or c-chart, depending on whether the area of opportunity varies.
debrief.wrong: Re-check the structure of each measure. Door-to-needle time is a measurement on a scale → continuous. Proportions screened or vaccinated are classification (each patient is yes or no). Needle-stick injuries are counts of events in a time window → count data.
debrief.rule_cited: Data structure → chart type — Provost & Murray ch. 5.

title: Outcome, process, or balancing?
brief:
A primary care team has set the aim: ‘Reduce the proportion of children under five who leave the clinic without their complete vaccination card updated, from 30% to under 10% within six months.’

A balanced family of measures usually has 1–2 outcome measures, 3–5 process measures, and 1–2 balancing measures. Match each candidate measure to its type.

task.stem: Match each candidate measure to its role in the family.

items.label: Proportion of under-five children leaving the clinic without an updated vaccination card.
Proportion of visits where the vaccination card is checked at intake.
Average minutes from arrival to vaccination card review.
Average waiting time per visit (to ensure the new step does not lengthen visits unduly).

debrief.correct: Good. The aim names the outcome (cards updated). Process measures look at how the system performs (cards checked at intake, time to review). Balancing measures watch for unintended consequences elsewhere — here, total waiting time.
debrief.wrong: Trace each measure back to the aim. Outcome = what we ultimately want to change (cards updated). Process = how the system is performing (cards checked, time to review). Balancing = what else might get worse if we focus only on the aim (waiting time).
debrief.rule_cited: Family of measures — IHI Model for Improvement (QI 102 / QI 103).

title: Order one PDSA cycle
brief:
Your team is planning a small test of change: have the triage nurse give every walk-in patient a printed wait-time estimate at registration. You want to test it Tuesday morning with two nurses and twenty patients.

Put these steps in the order a PDSA cycle should follow them.

task.stem: Drag the steps into the correct order.

steps.label: Predict: ‘We expect 80% of patients to receive an estimate, and that giving estimates will not delay registration.’
Plan: ‘Tuesday 8–11 a.m. Two nurses. Twenty patients. Estimates printed from the queue board.’
Do: Run the test on Tuesday morning; one observer notes what happens and what is missed.
Study: Compare the prediction (80% receive an estimate) with the observation (15 of 20 did).
Act: Decide to adopt, adapt (e.g. add a back-up estimate stamp), or abandon — and what to test next.

debrief.correct: Yes. A useful PDSA cycle starts with a clear **prediction** (what you expect to happen), then a tight **plan** (who, when, how much), then a short **Do**, a **Study** that compares prediction to observation, and an **Act** that decides whether to adopt, adapt, or abandon. Skipping the prediction is the single most common cause of weak PDSA cycles.
debrief.wrong: A PDSA cycle without an upfront **prediction** is just an audit. The order is: Predict, Plan, Do, Study, Act. The prediction is what makes the Study step meaningful: you are comparing what you expected to what actually happened.
debrief.rule_cited: PDSA cycle — IHI Model for Improvement (QI 103).

title: Classify the harm
brief:
Your safety officer asks you to triage four incident reports from the past week. Use the World Health Organization International Classification for Patient Safety (ICPS) harm-severity categories: **None, Mild, Moderate, Severe, Death**.

In the ICPS framing, the patient outcome is the anchor, not the *type* of event.

task.stem: Match each incident to the most appropriate ICPS harm category.

items.label: Wrong-dose paracetamol prescribed; pharmacist caught the error before dispensing; patient never received the wrong dose.
Patient received an antibiotic to which they had a documented allergy; developed a mild rash that resolved with antihistamines; no hospital stay required.
Post-operative haemorrhage requiring return to theatre and three-day ICU admission; patient recovered fully.
Maternal death from post-partum haemorrhage after delayed identification of bleeding.

debrief.correct: Good. In ICPS, severity is anchored on the **patient outcome**. A near-miss caught before reaching the patient is ‘None’. A transient symptom managed without significant intervention is ‘Mild’. Events requiring intervention to sustain life or extended hospitalisation are ‘Severe’. The category does not depend on the type of event or whether the cause was avoidable.
debrief.wrong: In ICPS, severity follows the patient outcome — not the type of event. A near-miss is ‘None’ regardless of how dangerous the drug was. An intervention to sustain life is ‘Severe’ even when recovery is full.
debrief.rule_cited: WHO ICPS harm severity categories.

title: Read a safety-culture survey
brief:
You receive the unit-level safety-culture survey results for the maternity ward at a faith-based district hospital. The bar chart below shows the **percentage of respondents agreeing or strongly agreeing** with each dimension.

The directorate has asked you to flag which dimension is the most concerning to start a conversation about.

exhibit.title: Safety-culture survey, maternity ward — percent positive by dimension

items.label: Teamwork
Supervisor support
Learning from errors
Communication openness
Non-punitive response
Handoffs & transitions

task.stem: Which dimension is most concerning, and what does that suggest about the unit?

options.label: Teamwork (82%) — there is room to grow.
Handoffs & transitions (69%) — patients move between shifts frequently here.
Non-punitive response (38%) — staff likely fear being blamed for errors, which suppresses reporting.
Learning from errors (71%) — it is the lowest of the three ‘learning’ dimensions.

debrief.correct: Yes. **Non-punitive response** is the lowest-scoring dimension by a wide margin, and a low score here typically means staff fear blame after an error. That fear suppresses incident reporting, which then biases every other safety measure you collect from this ward. It is also a leading indicator: low non-punitive scores often precede a drop in reported events without a real drop in events.
debrief.wrong: Look for the lowest-scoring dimension. **Non-punitive response (38%)** stands out. A low score here means staff fear being blamed, which suppresses incident reporting — and that biases your other safety data. A culture-of-safety conversation usually starts here, not with teamwork (already high).
debrief.rule_cited: Safety culture interpretation — WHO PS Curriculum Guide topic 5 (Learning from errors).

title: Read a leadership dashboard
brief: The {{exec}}’s monthly {{board}} includes the following four measures. Before you respond to them in the meeting, classify each as outcome, process, or balancing — that determines what kind of action makes sense.

task.stem: Tag each dashboard measure.

items.label: 30-day all-cause readmission rate.
Proportion of discharges with a documented medication reconciliation.
Average length of stay on the medical wards (in days).
Staff overtime hours per ward per month.

debrief.correct: Good. Outcomes describe how the system is performing for patients (readmissions, length of stay). Process measures track whether the care steps that drive outcomes are actually happening (medication reconciliation). Balancing measures watch for unintended harm from a focused initiative — here, that staff overtime might rise if you push wards to discharge faster.
debrief.wrong: The {{board}} usually contains a mix of measure types. Re-tag: readmissions and length-of-stay are outcomes (what happened to patients). Medication reconciliation is a process measure (did the step happen?). Overtime hours is a balancing measure (what else might worsen as we push other measures?).
debrief.rule_cited: Family of measures applied to leadership dashboards — IHI QI 102, NAHQ Quality Leadership & Integration domain.

title: When stratification changes the story
brief:
The district MoH dashboard reports the under-five **fully-immunised** coverage at **87%**, which looks well above the national 80% target. The {{exec2}} is preparing to congratulate the {{region}} immunisation team in the next quarterly review.

Before the meeting, the M&E officer shares the disaggregated figures below.

exhibit.title: Under-five full immunisation coverage by sub-district

task.stem: What should you tell the {{exec2}}?

options.label: Congratulate the team — 82% district average is above target, and stratification is just operational noise.
Re-check the maths — the district average looks inconsistent with the published 87%, and two sub-districts are under 60% despite the strong urban result.
Wait for next quarter — the sample sizes in the rural sub-districts are too small to act on.
Stratify by gender of child as well — equity is mainly about gender.

debrief.correct: Yes. The district headline (87% or 82%, depending on which number you trust) **hides** two sub-districts under 60%. Telling that story to the {{exec2}} — and acting on it — is the equity move. The reported headline also looks inconsistent with the disaggregated total, which is itself worth raising with whoever produced the dashboard. Equity stratification by geography, language, wealth, or gender is core to interpreting a system-level number, not an optional add-on.
debrief.wrong: An aggregate number can hide inequity that is the actual story. Here the urban result (94%) pulls the headline above target while the riverine and pastoralist sub-districts sit under 60%. Stratifying by where people live changes the question from ‘are we doing well overall?’ to ‘who is being left behind, and what will we do about it?’
debrief.rule_cited: Equity-stratified measurement — WHO Handbook for National Quality Policy and Strategy.

title: Pick the right chart for the audience
brief:
You have to present the same data three times this month: to the ward team in their handover (15 minutes, mostly nurses), to the directorate at the {{board_meeting}} (5 minutes, executives), and as a written brief for the regulator.

The data is the monthly proportion of surgical patients receiving the prophylactic-antibiotic-on-time bundle, over the past 18 months.

task.stem: Which approach is best for the **directorate at the quarterly governance / board meeting**?

options.label: Show the full p-chart with control limits, annotate the special-cause point, and explain ‘we saw a special-cause signal in March; the team identified delayed pharmacy delivery, fixed it; we’d like resources to embed the fix.’
Show eighteen raw data values in a table with three decimal places of precision.
Show a pie chart of the three reasons antibiotics were late.
Show the median value across all 18 months as a single number with no chart.

debrief.correct: Yes. Executives need to see (a) whether the system has changed (the chart), (b) whether anyone is acting on the change (the annotation), and (c) what they can decide on (the ask). A p-chart with one clear story and one ask is the canonical board-ready visualisation.
debrief.wrong: Audience drives the visual. A table of 18 raw values reads as noise to an executive in five minutes. A pie chart loses the time dimension. A single median number hides whether anything is improving. A p-chart with the signal annotated and a clear ask carries the story and earns the time you have.
debrief.rule_cited: Visual choice by audience — Provost & Murray ch. 7; IHI QI 104.

title: Find the shift signal
brief:
Your QI team has been working since March on improving the proportion of children under five with a malaria-positive RDT who are dispensed an artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) **on the same day** at a rural health centre. The chart below shows the last 20 weeks of weekly data.

Using Provost & Murray’s **shift rule** — six or more consecutive points on one side of the median signal a non-random change — click the points that make up the shift.

(Tip: keyboard users can press Tab to enter the chart, then Left/Right arrow to move between points, and Enter to select.)

exhibit.title: Same-day ACT dispensing for malaria-positive children U5 (weekly)

task.stem: Click each point that is part of the shift (the run of consecutive points entirely on one side of the median). Submit when you have the full shift selected.

debrief.correct: Spotted. Weeks 9–15 are all above the median (65%) — that is **seven** consecutive points above, which exceeds the threshold of six for the shift rule. The drop after week 15 is back into routine variation. A shift is one of the four classic run-chart signals; the others are trend, runs (too many / too few crossings of the median), and astronomical point.
debrief.wrong: The shift rule: **six or more consecutive points entirely on one side of the median** (points on the median do not count). Look for the run starting around week 9 — seven points are above the median (65%) before the chart drops back. The eye is often drawn to the peak (week 14, 76%), but the signal is the sustained run, not the maximum.
debrief.rule_cited: Provost & Murray (2nd ed.) — Shift rule (≥ 6 consecutive points on one side of the median).

title: Pick the right chart — and defend it
brief:
You are asked to chart the **proportion of post-partum mothers screened for depression before discharge**, monthly for 18 months, in a hospital where the **number of post-partum discharges varies each month** (anywhere from 80 to 250).

You have enough baseline data and the process appears stable. Choose the right control chart, then say why.

task.stem: Which chart type is the right choice here?

options.label: Run chart (median line; no control limits)
p-chart
u-chart
I-MR chart

task.reasonStem: Why that chart? Pick the best reason.

reasons.label: Because the underlying data are continuous values on a numeric scale.
Because each patient is classified yes/no and the subgroup size (denominator) varies each month, so the control limits must vary with subgroup size.
Because we are counting events in an area of opportunity and the area is constant.
Because run charts work for everything and are simpler to read.

debrief.correct: Right. The data are classifications (each mother is screened, yes/no), and the subgroup size (monthly discharges) varies — that is exactly when you reach for a **p-chart**, where the control limits **vary with the denominator** in each subgroup. A run chart could be used too, but with stable baseline and enough data, p-chart gives you control limits and signal rules a run chart cannot. A u-chart is for **count** data in an area of opportunity; I-MR is for **continuous individual values**.
debrief.wrong: Two clues drive the choice: (1) the data are classifications (yes/no per patient) → that points at a **p-chart**, not a u-chart (which is for counts) or an I-MR (which is for continuous). (2) The subgroup size varies — so the p-chart’s control limits must also vary subgroup-by-subgroup. A run chart would work but doesn’t give you control limits.
debrief.rule_cited: Chart selection by data structure — Provost & Murray ch. 5–6.

title: Build an operational definition
brief:
Your team has agreed the next measure: **proportion of post-partum mothers screened for depression before discharge**. Before you start collecting data, build the operational definition that an auditor at the next ward could read and reproduce.

Fill in each field. The system will accept reasonable phrasings — what matters is that each component is named and bounded.

task.stem: Build the operational definition.

fields.label: Numerator (what counts as a screened mother?)
fields.placeholder: e.g., mothers with a completed EPDS or PHQ-9 form before discharge…

fields.label: Denominator (who is in the eligible population?)
fields.placeholder: e.g., all post-partum mothers discharged from the maternity ward…

fields.label: Inclusions
fields.placeholder: e.g., includes singleton and multiple births, vaginal and caesarean…

fields.label: Exclusions
fields.placeholder: e.g., excludes mothers whose baby died before discharge, mothers leaving against advice…

fields.label: Data source
fields.placeholder: e.g., paper post-partum register; cross-checked with discharge folder…

fields.label: Measurement window
fields.placeholder: e.g., monthly; period = first to last day of calendar month…

debrief.correct: A working operational definition has six components: numerator, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, data source, and measurement window. Once those are named, two auditors in different wards should be able to count the same way. The most common mistakes: writing the numerator as ‘screening rate’ (that is the measure, not the numerator), forgetting exclusions, or leaving the data source vague.
debrief.wrong: Re-check that each field actually names a component: the **numerator** is the count of screened mothers (not the rate itself); the **denominator** is the eligible population (post-partum discharges); **inclusions** and **exclusions** bound the eligible population; **data source** names the register, chart, or system (e.g., HMIS / DHIS2); **measurement window** is the period (e.g., monthly).
debrief.rule_cited: Operational definitions — IHI QI 102, Provost & Murray ch. 3.

title: Build a balanced family of measures
brief:
Aim: **‘Reduce stockouts of essential medicines (per the national EML) at our six PHC clinics, from an average of 8 days per clinic per month to under 2 days per clinic per month, within six months.’**

You have six candidate measures. Choose a balanced family: ideally one or two outcome measures, three to five process measures, and one or two balancing measures.

task.stem: Tag each candidate measure.

items.label: Average stockout-days per clinic per month for essential medicines.
Proportion of weekly stock counts completed on time.
Proportion of clinics with a re-order point set and visible on each medicine shelf.
Days from re-order trigger to receipt of medicines at the clinic.
Number of expired medicines discarded per clinic per month (watching that we don’t over-order).
Patient-reported satisfaction with availability of prescribed medicines (post-visit survey).

debrief.correct: Good. **Outcome** measures sit closest to the aim and to the patient (stockout-days; patient-reported satisfaction). **Process** measures track whether the work that drives outcomes is happening (weekly counts, re-order points, re-supply lead time). **Balancing** measures watch for unintended consequences — here, that pushing harder on stock-on-hand might cause over-ordering and waste from expiry. A balanced family avoids the common trap of measuring only one process (e.g., on-time counts) and declaring success when the outcome hasn’t moved.
debrief.wrong: Trace each candidate back to the aim. Outcomes: stockout-days, patient satisfaction with availability. Processes: counts on time, re-order points set, re-supply lead time. Balancing: expired-medicines discarded (the thing that might worsen if we over-correct).
debrief.rule_cited: Family of measures — IHI Model for Improvement (QI 102).

title: Reading a Pareto of incident types
brief:
The patient-safety officer has classified the past quarter’s 138 reported incidents on the medical wards into the categories below. They want help deciding what the safety committee should focus on first.

Use the Pareto chart to identify the smallest set of categories that together account for the bulk of incidents.

exhibit.title: Incident reports by category, medical wards, past quarter (n=138)

items.label: Falls
Medication errors
Pressure injuries
IV / line issues
Communication
Documentation
Other

task.stem: What does this Pareto tell you to do first?

options.label: Investigate every category equally — they are all incident reports.
Start a focused effort on falls and medication errors, which together account for about 60% of reports; design improvements at the system level, not for individual staff.
Wait for the next quarter — three months is too short to draw conclusions from any Pareto.
Reclassify everything as ‘Other’ because the categories overlap.

debrief.correct: Yes. A Pareto is a way of saying ‘not everything is equal — start where the volume is.’ Here falls (48) and medication errors (36) are 84 of 138 reports — about 61% of the load. A safety committee that designs system-level improvements for those two categories does more good than one that distributes its attention evenly across seven categories. (And yes, three months can be enough to act if your reporting culture is mature; if it isn’t, work on the reporting culture first.)
debrief.wrong: A Pareto chart focuses scarce attention. The cumulative line shows that falls + medication errors together account for roughly 61% of all reports. Designing system-level improvements for those two categories has more impact than spreading effort evenly across seven. Categories with very small counts (Documentation, Other) can wait.
debrief.rule_cited: Pareto principle in QI — Provost & Murray ch. 8; WHO PS Curriculum topic 6.

title: The board wants a target line on the control chart
brief:
At the {{board_meeting}} last week, the {{exec}} asked you to ‘draw the 90% target line across the control chart so we can see whether we are missing it.’

The chart on screen is the p-chart below — proportion of inpatient discharges with a completed medication reconciliation, by month. The team wants advice before next week’s meeting.

exhibit.title: Medication reconciliation completion at discharge — monthly p-chart

task.stem: How do you respond to the {{exec}}?

options.label: Draw the 90% line across as the upper control limit; explain that any month above the line is a special-cause signal.
Decline the request: a target is not a control limit; instead, annotate the target on a run-chart view of the same data, and explain what the p-chart’s control limits do say.
Re-compute the control limits using 90% as the centre line, so the chart shows whether we are at target.
Remove the control limits entirely and show only the data points.

reasons.label: Because targets and control limits answer different questions: targets are aspirational; control limits describe the natural variation of the current system. Confusing them invites the wrong action.
Because the board owns the chart and can set whatever lines they like.
Because medication reconciliation is too complex to chart at all.
Because control limits should only be drawn when at least 24 baseline data points exist.

debrief.correct: Exactly. **A target line is not a control limit.** Control limits describe the natural variation of the current system; a target describes where you want the system to be. Drawing the target as a UCL would re-label every month above it as ‘special cause’ — which it is not — and pull the team into chasing false signals. The right move is to keep the p-chart (with its proper, subgroup-varying control limits) and **annotate the target on a run-chart view** of the same data, or in commentary alongside it. The conversation then becomes: ‘The current system is centred near 84%; reaching 90% will require a deliberate change. Here is what we propose to test.’
debrief.wrong: This is the most common dashboard misuse in healthcare leadership reporting. **Control limits describe the system as it currently behaves**; **targets describe where leaders want it to be**. They are not interchangeable, and drawing a target as a UCL turns ordinary monthly variation into false ‘special cause’ alarms. Keep the p-chart with its proper limits, **annotate the target separately**, and use the gap between the current centre line and the target to drive a change plan.
debrief.rule_cited: Targets vs control limits — Provost & Murray ch. 5 (and the ‘category error’ caveat called out in IHI QI 104).

title: Build a driver diagram
brief:
Aim: **'Reduce the rate of surgical-site infections (SSI) at Abubakar District Hospital from 14% to below 4% within 9 months.'**

The improvement team has agreed on three primary drivers:
- **Primary Driver 1 — Pre-operative preparation**
- **Primary Driver 2 — Intraoperative sterile technique**
- **Primary Driver 3 — Post-operative wound care**

Six change ideas have been proposed. Place each idea under the primary driver it most directly addresses.

exhibit.title: SSI prevention driver diagram
exhibit.aim: Reduce surgical-site infections from 14% to below 4% within 9 months.

task.stem: Match each change idea to its primary driver.

items.label: Introduce a pre-operative chlorhexidine skin-scrub checklist for all elective surgical patients.
Add a daily wound-inspection chart to each post-operative patient's bedside folder.
Train scrub nurses to call a stop if sterility is broken during a procedure.
Give patients an education card on wound warning signs before discharge.
Create a standard procedure for giving prophylactic antibiotics before the incision.
Introduce a double instrument count at the start and close of every operation.

debrief.correct: Correct. In a driver diagram, change ideas sit directly below the primary driver they address — the upstream cause they act on. **Pre-operative ideas** (skin prep checklist, prophylactic antibiotic procedure) reduce the risk of contamination before the incision. **Intraoperative ideas** (sterility stop, instrument count) maintain a clean field during the operation itself. **Post-operative ideas** (wound chart, discharge education card) detect and contain problems after the wound is closed. Placing an idea under the wrong driver breaks the causal logic the diagram is designed to make visible — and can lead a team to test a change in the wrong phase of care.
debrief.wrong: Ask: at what phase of care does this idea act? Pre-op ideas happen before the incision (skin prep, prophylactic antibiotics). Intraop ideas happen during the operation (sterility checks, instrument counts). Post-op ideas happen after wound closure (daily wound monitoring, patient education on warning signs). Match the idea to its phase, and you have matched it to its primary driver.
debrief.rule_cited: Driver diagram — IHI Model for Improvement (QI 102); change package construction.

title: Presenting data to your frontline team
brief:
You are the Quality Lead at a monthly facility in-charge meeting. You have 12 months of data on the proportion of children under five screened for malnutrition at each visit. The run chart shows a clear downward shift starting in month 7 — six consecutive months below the median — meaning screening has worsened consistently.

Your audience is a team of ten Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) who do the screening. They have not had statistics training. You have five minutes.

task.stem: Which approach gives the CHEWs the most useful information in the time available?

options.label: Show the run chart, circle the six points below the median, and say: 'Screening dropped consistently from July onwards. We need to find out why together.'
Read out all 12 monthly percentage values from a printed table.
Show only the annual average and compare it to the national target.
Show a pie chart splitting the reasons for missed screenings.

debrief.correct: Yes. The run chart with the shift circled tells the CHEWs exactly when the problem started and how long it has lasted — the two things they need to generate ideas about the cause. A plain-language caption converts the statistical signal into a statement any team member can act on, without statistical training. Frontline workers who see their own data in a clear visual are far more likely to engage with improvement than those who receive a summary number.
debrief.wrong: Match the visual to what the audience needs to do next. CHEWs need to see that something changed, roughly when it changed, and that they are expected to help explain it. A table of 12 values requires mental arithmetic they should not have to do in five minutes. A single annual average hides the time pattern — it would mask the shift entirely if the first six months were strong. A pie chart of reasons is useful, but only after the team agrees there is a sustained problem to investigate. The run chart with the shift marked is the bridge between the data and the team's own experience of what changed in July.
debrief.rule_cited: Visual choice by audience — Provost & Murray ch. 7; IHI QI 104; WHO NQPS data use for frontline teams.

title: SQHN Post-Survey: Identifying the Priority Domain
brief: A 120-bed district hospital in Kaduna State, Nigeria has received its post-survey report from the Society for Quality in Healthcare in Nigeria (SQHN). Four domains were scored: Clinical Governance 62%, Patient Safety 44%, Information Management 68%, and Human Resources 57%. The hospital quality team must decide where to focus first.

task.stem: Which domain should the hospital prioritise first, and what is the correct immediate data action?

options.label: Patient Safety — it scored the lowest at 44% and carries the highest risk of harm to patients; the immediate action is to audit the specific Patient Safety sub-standards that were flagged and begin a corrective data collection plan.
Clinical Governance — it scored 62%, which is the second lowest, so it is nearly as urgent as Patient Safety and should be addressed before the others.
Information Management — it scored the highest at 68%, so improvements here will boost the overall score most efficiently.
Human Resources — staffing problems affect all other domains, so fixing Human Resources first will automatically improve the other scores.

debrief.correct: Patient Safety at 44% is the lowest-scoring domain and the one most directly linked to patient harm. SQHN standards align with the principle that patient safety deficiencies require immediate corrective action. The right first step is to audit the sub-standards that failed inspection and design a targeted data collection plan to track improvement. SQHN is a Nigerian national accreditation body whose standards are accredited by the International Society for Quality in Health Care External Evaluation Association (ISQua-IEEA), placing them at the same international level of rigour as JCI, COHSASA, and Accreditation Canada.
debrief.wrong: Clinical Governance at 62% is important but is not the lowest-scoring domain and does not carry the same immediate patient-harm risk as Patient Safety. Information Management at 68% is actually the highest-scoring domain — selecting the top-scoring domain as the priority contradicts the principle of addressing the greatest gap and risk first. Human Resources at 57% matters for sustainability, but staffing issues do not automatically resolve patient safety failures; those sub-standards must be addressed directly and specifically.
debrief.rule_cited: SQHN accreditation standards require a corrective action plan for each domain scored below the accreditation threshold, prioritised by patient risk.

title: COHSASA Survey Prep: Closing the Data Gap
brief: A hospital in Lusaka, Zambia is three months away from its Council for Health Service Accreditation of Southern Africa (COHSASA) survey. COHSASA standards require 12 months of data for six core indicators. The hospital has complete 12-month data for four indicators, but only three months of data for two: the maternal mortality ratio and the nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection rate.

task.stem: Which action best addresses the data gap before the survey?

options.label: Begin prospective data collection immediately for the two incomplete indicators, document the gap transparently in the self-assessment with a clear explanation, and attach a corrective action plan with a realistic timeline.
Use the three months of available data to calculate an estimate for the missing nine months and submit those estimated values alongside the complete indicators.
Wait and see — the surveyor may not ask about those two indicators during the visit.
Submit only the four complete indicators and say nothing about the other two in the self-assessment report.

debrief.correct: Starting data collection immediately gives the hospital three months of real data before the survey. Transparent disclosure in the self-assessment, supported by a corrective action plan, shows COHSASA surveyors that the facility recognises the gap and is actively addressing it. Honesty with a credible plan is always preferred over silence or false data. COHSASA is one of a small group of African accreditation bodies whose standards are accredited by ISQua-IEEA, meaning its requirements reflect international best practice.
debrief.wrong: Estimating or extrapolating values for missing months is a form of data fabrication, which can result in disqualification from accreditation and loss of trust. Hoping the surveyor will not ask about required indicators is not a safe strategy — COHSASA surveyors check all six core indicators as a mandatory part of the survey process. Submitting only the complete indicators without explaining the gap is treated as an incomplete and potentially misleading submission, which surveyors will flag as a finding; concealment is worse than transparent disclosure.
debrief.rule_cited: COHSASA standards require 12 months of complete data for all designated core indicators; gaps must be disclosed in the self-assessment with a corrective action plan.

title: SafeCare Level 2: What Does It Mean and What Comes Next?
brief: A private clinic in Lagos, Nigeria has completed its first SafeCare assessment and scored at Level 2 out of a possible 5 levels. The clinic director wants to know what Level 2 means for the clinic and what the next steps should be.

task.stem: Which response best answers the clinic director's question about Level 2 and what to do next?

options.label: Level 2 means the clinic meets basic safety standards. SafeCare uses a stepwise model: the clinic should review the Level 3 requirements in the assessment report and begin implementing them before the next assessment.
Level 2 is the highest level a clinic can reach in its first assessment year, so no further action is needed until the next scheduled assessment.
Level 2 means the clinic failed the assessment and should reapply from Level 1 at the next cycle.
Level 2 has no practical meaning until the clinic reaches Level 5, so no action should be taken at this stage.

debrief.correct: SafeCare, developed by the PharmAccess Foundation, uses a five-level stepwise model. Each level confirms that a facility meets a defined set of safety and quality standards, and each step builds on the last. Level 2 is a genuine achievement — it confirms the clinic has met basic safety requirements — but it is not a stopping point. The clinic should use the detailed assessment report to identify which Level 3 requirements are not yet met and begin working on them immediately. SafeCare is used widely in West, East, and Southern Africa and is recognised by ISQua-IEEA.
debrief.wrong: There is no rule that limits clinics to Level 2 in their first year — some facilities progress faster depending on their readiness. Level 2 is not a failure; it confirms real progress and provides a clear pathway to Level 3. Waiting for no reason between levels contradicts the continuous improvement model that underpins SafeCare. Stating that Level 2 has no practical meaning is incorrect: each level signals compliance with a specific set of standards and unlocks access to further support from the SafeCare program.
debrief.rule_cited: SafeCare's stepwise assessment model requires facilities to achieve each level sequentially, with each level building on verified compliance from the previous one.

title: NHIA Renewal: Protecting Accreditation with Incomplete Data
brief: A hospital in Kano, Nigeria is renewing its accreditation with the Nigeria Health Insurance Authority (NHIA). NHIA requires quarterly submission of five indicators: bed occupancy rate, average length of stay, nosocomial infection rate, maternal mortality ratio, and under-5 mortality rate. The hospital's health management information system (HMIS) has complete data for three of the five indicators, but the nosocomial infection rate and under-5 mortality rate have not been routinely collected.

task.stem: Which action best protects the hospital's accreditation eligibility during the renewal process?

options.label: Submit data for the three available indicators, include a written explanation for the two missing indicators, and attach a corrective action plan with a clear timeline for establishing routine data collection.
Calculate estimated values for the two missing indicators based on national averages and submit them alongside the three complete indicators.
Request an extension from NHIA without submitting any data, so there is more time to collect the missing indicators.
Submit only the three complete indicators with no mention of the other two, to avoid drawing attention to the gap.

debrief.correct: Submitting verified data for the three available indicators, explaining the gap honestly, and providing a corrective action plan demonstrates good faith and administrative transparency. NHIA reviewers are trained to distinguish between facilities that acknowledge and address gaps and those that conceal them. A credible plan with a realistic timeline is treated as evidence of a functioning quality system, not as grounds for immediate penalty.
debrief.wrong: Submitting estimated or nationally averaged values in place of facility-specific data is data fabrication. If discovered, this can result in immediate revocation of accreditation eligibility. Requesting an extension without submitting anything leaves the hospital formally non-compliant for the entire extension period, which creates its own risk. Submitting an incomplete report with no explanation is treated as a non-compliant submission — NHIA reviewers will identify the missing required indicators and flag the omission as more serious than a disclosed gap would have been.
debrief.rule_cited: NHIA accreditation standards require quarterly submission of all five designated core indicators; undisclosed gaps in required data are treated as non-compliance.

title: ISQua-IEEA Meta-Accreditation: What It Means for SQHN-Accredited Hospitals
brief: A quality officer at a Nigerian hospital is briefing hospital leadership. The hospital holds accreditation from the Society for Quality in Healthcare in Nigeria (SQHN). The chief executive officer has asked: 'ISQua-IEEA accredits SQHN's standards — what does that actually mean for our hospital?'

task.stem: Which explanation correctly describes what ISQua-IEEA meta-accreditation means for a hospital accredited by SQHN?

options.label: ISQua-IEEA has independently evaluated SQHN's standards and processes and confirmed they meet globally recognised criteria. An SQHN accreditation therefore signals the same level of standards rigour as accreditation by JCI, COHSASA, or Accreditation Canada — these bodies are in the same international class.
SQHN is a branch of ISQua, and all individual survey decisions made by SQHN are reviewed and approved by ISQua before they take effect.
ISQua-IEEA membership automatically gives the hospital accreditation status with all other ISQua member bodies worldwide, so no separate surveys are needed.
ISQua sets Nigeria's accreditation standards directly, and SQHN's role is to implement those standards as written by ISQua.

debrief.correct: The International Society for Quality in Health Care External Evaluation Association (ISQua-IEEA) functions as the 'accreditor of accreditors.' It evaluates whether a national or regional accreditation body's standards, surveyor training, and processes meet an internationally agreed set of criteria. Bodies that pass this evaluation — including SQHN, COHSASA, JCI, Accreditation Canada, and ACHS — form a small global club whose accreditation programmes are considered equivalent in rigour. For the hospital, this means that SQHN accreditation carries credibility beyond Nigeria's borders and is recognised in cross-border quality comparisons and donor reporting.
debrief.wrong: SQHN is an independent Nigerian body; ISQua-IEEA does not sit above it in a chain of command or review its individual survey decisions. The meta-accreditation process evaluates the standards and systems, not the outcomes of specific surveys. ISQua-IEEA membership does not transfer accreditation status between bodies — each accreditation body surveys facilities separately, and a hospital must apply to each body independently. ISQua does not write Nigeria's standards; SQHN develops its own standards, and ISQua-IEEA evaluates them against international criteria.
debrief.rule_cited: ISQua-IEEA meta-accreditation confirms that an accreditation body's standards and processes meet international criteria; it does not transfer accreditation between bodies or review individual survey decisions.

title: JCI IPSG: Identifying the Breached International Patient Safety Goal
brief: A 150-bed private hospital in Nairobi, Kenya is accredited by Joint Commission International (JCI). A patient received a blood transfusion that had been prepared for a different patient. No serious harm resulted, and the near-miss was reported through the incident reporting system. The quality team must document which International Patient Safety Goal (IPSG) was primarily breached.

task.stem: Which IPSG does this incident primarily relate to?

options.label: IPSG 1 — Correctly Identifying Patients. The transfusion was prepared for the wrong patient, indicating a failure of patient identification at the point of specimen collection or at the bedside before administration.
IPSG 2 — Improving Effective Communication. A handover communication failure was the root cause, so this is primarily a communication breakdown rather than an identification failure.
IPSG 3 — Improving the Safety of High-Alert Medications. Blood products are classified as high-alert items, so any transfusion error is primarily a medication safety incident.
IPSG 6 — Reducing the Risk of Patient Harm Resulting from Falls. This goal covers any incident in which a patient could have been harmed during their admission.

debrief.correct: IPSG 1 requires at least two patient identifiers to be checked at every point of care, including at specimen collection and at the bedside immediately before a transfusion begins. A blood product prepared for the wrong patient is a classic IPSG 1 failure. JCI's six IPSGs are: IPSG 1 Correctly Identifying Patients, IPSG 2 Improving Effective Communication, IPSG 3 Improving the Safety of High-Alert Medications, IPSG 4 Ensuring Correct-Site Correct-Procedure Correct-Patient Surgery, IPSG 5 Reducing the Risk of Healthcare-Associated Infections, and IPSG 6 Reducing the Risk of Patient Harm Resulting from Falls. Transfusion errors due to patient mis-identification are among the most preventable serious adverse events in healthcare.
debrief.wrong: IPSG 2 covers breakdowns in handover communication — for example, verbal orders or discharge summaries — but the root cause here is failure to verify which patient the blood product belongs to, not a communication gap between staff. IPSG 3 covers high-alert medications such as concentrated electrolytes and anticoagulants; while blood products require careful handling, the error in this case is identification, not medication management. IPSG 6 is specifically about falls prevention and has no connection to a transfusion incident.
debrief.rule_cited: JCI IPSG 1 requires staff to use at least two patient identifiers when providing care, treatment, or services, including at the point of blood product administration.

title: Accreditation Canada ROP: Responding to a Medication Reconciliation Finding
brief: A hospital pursuing Accreditation Canada Diamond accreditation has received its preliminary survey report. The report flags that there is no documented medication reconciliation process at admission — this is a Required Organizational Practice (ROP). The hospital has 90 days to submit a formal response.

task.stem: Which response correctly addresses the Required Organizational Practice finding within the 90-day window?

options.label: Treat this as a mandatory gap: develop and implement a medication reconciliation process within 90 days, collect compliance data from the first day of implementation, and submit evidence of improvement at the follow-up review.
Treat it as an advisory finding — Required Organizational Practices are recommendations, so the hospital can address it in its own time without risking its accreditation status.
Request a waiver from Accreditation Canada on the grounds that the hospital's patient population is low-risk and medication errors are unlikely.
Begin planning the process after the 90-day window has closed and explain the delay in a letter, as the planning phase itself is evidence of good intent.

debrief.correct: Required Organizational Practices (ROPs) are Accreditation Canada's non-negotiable patient safety practices. They are based on evidence that implementing them reduces the risk of serious harm. Failure to meet an ROP within the required timeframe can result in a conditional or non-accredited status. Medication reconciliation is one of several ROPs — others include falls prevention strategies, hand hygiene audits, and safe surgery checklists. Diamond accreditation, Accreditation Canada's highest level, requires all ROPs to be fully met. Collecting data from day one of implementation allows the hospital to demonstrate a measurable improvement trajectory rather than a single endpoint result.
debrief.wrong: ROPs are requirements, not recommendations. There is no discretion about whether to address them, and they carry clear accreditation consequences if unmet. Accreditation Canada does not grant waivers for ROPs based on perceived patient risk — the evidence base for each ROP applies across all settings. Beginning action after the 90-day window has closed is a formal non-compliance, and a letter explaining the delay does not substitute for a corrective action completed within the required period.
debrief.rule_cited: Accreditation Canada's Required Organizational Practices are mandatory; failure to address an ROP finding within the specified response window affects accreditation status.

title: CQC Single Assessment Framework: Responding to a 'Requires Improvement' Rating
brief: An NHS trust in England has received its Care Quality Commission (CQC) assessment under the Single Assessment Framework (SAF). The 'Safe' quality theme has been rated 'Requires Improvement.' The trust quality director asks the quality improvement (QI) team which data they should review first and what action they should take.

task.stem: Which action best responds to this CQC finding in the 'Safe' theme?

options.label: Review the specific Quality Statements within the 'Safe' theme that were rated as 'Requires Improvement,' identify what evidence or data was absent or weak, and build an improvement plan with measurable targets against those specific statements.
Appeal the overall 'Safe' rating to CQC before doing anything else, since the rating may be based on incomplete information.
Collect data across all five SAF themes simultaneously to show CQC that the trust is committed to improvement across the board.
Wait for the next scheduled CQC inspection before acting, as any changes made now will not be assessed until then anyway.

debrief.correct: The CQC Single Assessment Framework (SAF) organises assessment around five quality themes: Safe, Effective, Caring, Responsive, and Well-led. Within each theme, specific Quality Statements describe what good practice looks like. When a theme is rated 'Requires Improvement,' the first action is to review which individual Quality Statements drove that rating and identify the specific evidence gaps. The four rating levels are Outstanding, Good, Requires Improvement, and Inadequate. Quality Statements replaced the previous Key Lines of Enquiry (KLOEs) under the SAF. A focused, evidence-based improvement plan linked to the flagged statements is what CQC expects to see.
debrief.wrong: Appealing a rating does not substitute for taking corrective action; CQC expects responsive improvement regardless of whether an appeal is filed, and appeals have a high threshold. Collecting data across all five themes simultaneously spreads resources thinly and ignores the specific finding — the trust knows that 'Safe' is the priority. Waiting for the next scheduled inspection before acting is a serious error: unaddressed 'Requires Improvement' findings can escalate to an 'Inadequate' rating and trigger enforcement action, including special measures, before the next planned assessment.
debrief.rule_cited: Under the CQC Single Assessment Framework, trusts rated 'Requires Improvement' in any theme are expected to produce and implement a responsive improvement plan linked to the specific Quality Statements that drove the rating.

title: ACHS EQuIP National: Building an Improvement Trajectory for Patient Experience Data
brief: A hospital in Brisbane, Australia is preparing for its Australian Council on Healthcare Standards (ACHS) EQuIP National survey. The self-assessment against the 'Partnering with Consumers' standard shows that 38% of required patient experience data points are currently being collected. The standard requires at least 80%. The survey is four months away.

task.stem: Which approach best demonstrates genuine improvement by the time of the survey?

options.label: Implement a systematic patient experience survey at every discharge starting immediately, report the monthly collection rate to the quality committee, document the improvement trajectory with a run chart, and present the improvement story — not just the final number — to the surveyor.
Revise the self-assessment target downward from 80% to 40% to match the hospital's current level of performance, then demonstrate 100% compliance with the revised target.
Collect a concentrated burst of patient experience surveys in the week immediately before the survey to reach 80% for that week alone.
Submit the self-assessment as it stands without addressing the gap, and explain to the surveyor that four months is not enough time to make a meaningful improvement.

debrief.correct: ACHS EQuIP National is the current accreditation programme of the Australian Council on Healthcare Standards. The 'Partnering with Consumers' standard reflects the principle that health services must actively collect and use patient experience data to improve care. ACHS surveyors are trained to look for improvement trajectories — a run chart showing month-by-month growth from 38% toward 80% is strong evidence of a genuine and sustained quality improvement effort. Starting at once, reporting monthly, and presenting the data story is far more compelling than a single end-point number. Four months of real data, well documented, is meaningful evidence.
debrief.wrong: ACHS sets the standards, not individual hospitals; the 80% threshold cannot be revised to match current performance — doing so would misrepresent the self-assessment and undermine its purpose. Collecting surveys only in the week before the survey creates an artificial spike that surveyors will detect when they review trend data over time; this approach may also raise integrity concerns. Explaining that four months is insufficient without providing any evidence of action or a credible plan will be assessed as an inadequate response to a known gap — surveyors expect initiative, not inaction.
debrief.rule_cited: ACHS EQuIP National requires facilities to demonstrate ongoing improvement against standard requirements; surveyors assess the quality of the improvement trajectory, not only the final compliance figure.

title: Abstract a prophylactic antibiotic record
brief:
Your hospital is auditing compliance with the prophylactic antibiotic measure for surgical patients. The measure criterion is: **a prophylactic antibiotic must be documented as given within 60 minutes before the skin incision.**

Review the patient record below. Then complete the abstraction form.

task.stem: Complete the abstraction form using the patient record above.

record.title: Patient Record — Case #D-14 · General Surgery Ward

fields.label: Is this case eligible for abstraction? (Inpatient surgery, patient ≥ 18 years, procedure on the measure list)

options.label: Yes — eligible
No — exclude from measure

fields.label: Was a prophylactic antibiotic ordered before the operation?

options.label: Yes
No
Unable to determine from the record

fields.label: Is the administration time documented so you can check the 60-minute criterion?

options.label: Yes — time is recorded
No — administration time is missing

fields.label: What is the correct abstraction result for this case?

options.label: Criterion met — antibiotic given within 60 minutes of incision
Criterion not met — antibiotic not given within 60 minutes
Exclude from measure — insufficient data to determine timing

debrief.correct: Correct. The antibiotic was ordered, but the administration time was never recorded. Without a documented time, you cannot determine whether the 60-minute criterion was met. The correct abstraction result is **exclude** — not 'met' and not 'not met'. Counting this case as a failure would unfairly penalise the team if the antibiotic was actually given on time. Counting it as a pass would inflate the compliance rate. Exclusion flags the documentation gap so it can be fixed.
debrief.wrong: Trace through each field. The case is eligible (inpatient surgery, adult, appendectomy is on the measure list). An antibiotic was ordered (Cefazolin 1 g IV at 09:15). But the administration time is not recorded — so you cannot calculate the interval to the 10:45 incision. When you cannot determine timing from the record, the correct abstraction is 'exclude from measure due to insufficient data' — not 'met' (you do not know) and not 'not met' (you also do not know).
debrief.rule_cited: Chart abstraction — data completeness and exclusion rules. NAHQ HQ Essentials: Chart Abstraction for Quality Measurement.

title: Design a chart audit
brief: Your district hospital wants to audit compliance with the hand hygiene (HH) policy. The aim is to estimate the current compliance rate across all wards. There are 8 wards, each with 4–6 clinical staff per shift. Audits must be done by a trained observer. You have one trained observer available for 2 hours per week.

task.stem: Which audit design best fits this aim and these constraints?

options.label: Systematic random sample: observe every 3rd opportunity across all wards during the 2 hours each week; rotate start ward weekly to avoid bias.
Observe all hand hygiene opportunities in Ward 1 only for the full 2 hours each week, then report a hospital-wide rate.
Ask each ward in-charge to self-report their ward's compliance rate at the end of the month.
Observe all 8 wards simultaneously by dividing 15 minutes per ward.

debrief.correct: Yes. A systematic random sample spread across all wards — with ward rotation — gives you a defensible hospital-wide estimate within your resource constraint. It avoids the two main biases: convenience bias (always observing the most accessible ward) and Hawthorne effect clustering (staff in one ward learn they are being watched and change behaviour, inflating the rate).
debrief.wrong: Observing only one ward gives a ward rate, not a hospital-wide rate — it cannot be generalised. Self-reporting by ward in-charges is not an audit; it is self-assessment, which consistently overestimates compliance because of social-desirability bias. Splitting 15 minutes across 8 wards simultaneously requires 8 observers — you have one. The only feasible design that covers the whole hospital is a systematic sample with rotation, even if each week's sample is small.
debrief.rule_cited: Audit sampling design — NAHQ HQ Essentials; IHI QI 102 measurement planning.

title: Classify a case for M&M review
brief:
Your hospital's Morbidity and Mortality (M&M) committee meets monthly to review adverse events. The committee's criteria for mandatory review are: **(1)** unexpected in-hospital death, **(2)** return to theatre within 30 days of a planned procedure, or **(3)** any complication rated as Severe or higher on the WHO ICPS harm scale.

A 58-year-old man underwent elective hernia repair. On day 3 post-operation he developed a surgical-site infection. He was treated with antibiotics and discharged on day 8. No further complications were recorded.

task.stem: Should this case be referred for M&M review?

options.label: Yes — a surgical-site infection is a complication. Classify harm severity first; refer if it meets the Severe threshold.
No — the patient recovered and was discharged; complications that resolve do not meet M&M criteria.
Yes — all post-operative complications are automatically referred for M&M review.
No — M&M review is only for deaths; this patient survived.

debrief.correct: Correct. A surgical-site infection is a complication, so the next step is to classify its harm severity using the WHO ICPS scale (None / Mild / Moderate / Severe / Death). A day-3 SSI treated with antibiotics, resolved by day 8, is most likely Moderate harm — which does not trigger the mandatory Severe threshold. However, you must classify first; you cannot skip the severity step and assume it is below the threshold. If the committee uses a lower threshold (e.g., Moderate and above), the answer changes — always apply your hospital's defined criteria.
debrief.wrong: Recovering does not mean a complication is exempt from review. The criteria are not limited to deaths (option D). Not all complications trigger M&M — only those meeting defined harm thresholds (option C is too broad). Option B skips the severity classification step, which is required before deciding. The correct process is: identify complication → classify severity → apply the committee's threshold criteria → refer if met.
debrief.rule_cited: M&M classification — WHO ICPS harm severity scale; NAHQ HQ Essentials: Peer Review.

title: Spot the reliability problem
brief:
Two trained abstractors independently reviewed the same 10 patient records for a hand-hygiene compliance audit. Their results for 5 of the records are shown below. For each record, decide whether the pair's results indicate a **reliability problem** or **no reliability problem**.

Reliability problem = the two abstractors reached different conclusions on whether the criterion was met, was not met, or was uncodeable.

task.stem: Classify each record pair.

items.label: Record #1 — Abstractor A: Met · Abstractor B: Met
Record #2 — Abstractor A: Not met · Abstractor B: Exclude (missing data)
Record #3 — Abstractor A: Met · Abstractor B: Not met
Record #4 — Abstractor A: Exclude · Abstractor B: Exclude
Record #5 — Abstractor A: Not met · Abstractor B: Not met

debrief.correct: Correct. Records #1, #4, and #5 show agreement between abstractors — same conclusion, no problem. Records #2 and #3 show disagreement. Record #2 is a subtle case: 'Not met' and 'Exclude' are different conclusions. One abstractor decided the criterion was failed; the other decided there was not enough data to judge. These require adjudication — a senior reviewer or a third abstractor must resolve the discrepancy before the data can be used.
debrief.wrong: Agreement means both abstractors reached the same conclusion — 'Met/Met', 'Not met/Not met', or 'Exclude/Exclude'. Any mix of different codes is a reliability problem, even when the codes are 'similar' (like 'Not met' vs 'Exclude'). Record #2 is the hardest: 'Not met' and 'Exclude' sound like near-agreement, but they carry different implications for the measure rate and the improvement response. Always treat different codes as a reliability flag.
debrief.rule_cited: Inter-rater reliability — chart abstraction training and adjudication. NAHQ HQ Essentials.

title: Interpret an audit report finding
brief:
A district hospital ran a monthly clinical audit on postnatal care documentation. The measure: **proportion of postnatal women with a completed postnatal check recorded within 6 hours of delivery.** The audit covered 40 records over 4 weeks.

| Week | Records audited | Criterion met | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Week 1 | 10 | 4 | 40% |
| Week 2 | 10 | 6 | 60% |
| Week 3 | 10 | 3 | 30% |
| Week 4 | 10 | 5 | 50% |

**Overall: 18 of 40 = 45%.** The hospital target is 90%.

task.stem: Which interpretation and next action is most appropriate?

options.label: The 45% overall rate is well below the 90% target, but the variation across weeks (30–60%) suggests the problem is inconsistent — not a uniform failure. The priority action is to investigate the process: when and why do checks get missed, and is it the same staff, shift, or day of the week each time?
The audit shows the hospital is improving: 40% in Week 1, 50% in Week 4. Continue monitoring and the target will be reached in time.
The overall rate is 45%, which is too low. The correct response is to set a higher target — 95% — to motivate the team.
Four weeks is too short to draw any conclusion. Repeat the audit for 3 months before taking any action.

debrief.correct: Correct. The 45% rate is a significant gap from 90%, and the week-to-week variation (30%–60%) is the key signal — it tells you the system is inconsistent, not uniformly failing. That inconsistency is a diagnostic clue: something is different on some days or shifts. Investigating *when* and *why* failures cluster is the right first step before designing an intervention. A run chart over more weeks would reveal whether the variation is random or patterned.
debrief.wrong: Option B misreads the data as a trend: Week 1 = 40%, Week 4 = 50% — but Weeks 2 and 3 go up then down. There is no consistent upward trend; that is common-cause variation. Option C confuses motivation with system design — raising a target never fixes a process. Option D delays action unnecessarily; 40 records is enough to identify a serious gap and begin investigation, even if more data will sharpen the picture.
debrief.rule_cited: Audit interpretation — common-cause vs assignable-cause variation. Provost & Murray ch. 3; IHI QI 104.

title: Apply a peer review classification
brief:
Your hospital's peer review committee uses a 3-level preventability classification:

- **Level 1 — Not preventable:** The adverse outcome was not avoidable given the information and resources available at the time.
- **Level 2 — Possibly preventable:** Different care *might* have changed the outcome, but there is reasonable uncertainty.
- **Level 3 — Preventable:** The evidence clearly shows that different, feasible care would likely have prevented the adverse outcome.

**Case summary:** A 42-year-old woman with known penicillin allergy was prescribed amoxicillin post-operatively. The allergy was documented in the paper medication chart but not transferred to the ward drug kardex. She received one dose before a nurse noticed the discrepancy. No adverse reaction occurred.

task.stem: Which preventability classification is most appropriate, and why?

options.label: Level 3 — Preventable. The allergy was documented; the failure was a transferable, system-level transcription step that did not happen. A feasible process (allergy check at kardex completion) would likely have prevented the prescribing error.
Level 1 — Not preventable. The allergy information existed but the prescriber could not have known it was missing from the kardex.
Level 2 — Possibly preventable. Because no adverse reaction occurred, the clinical harm is uncertain and so the preventability is uncertain.
Level 3 — Preventable. The prescriber should have checked the original medication chart before prescribing.

debrief.correct: Correct — Level 3. The allergy was documented. The failure was a specific, identifiable system gap: allergy information was not transferred from the paper medication chart to the ward drug kardex. A feasible process fix — a mandatory allergy-transfer check at kardex completion, or a single source of truth — would likely have prevented this. Preventability classification is about the *process and system*, not about whether the patient was harmed. Near-misses can be Level 3.
debrief.wrong: Option B (Level 1) treats this as unavoidable, but the information *was available* — it just was not in the right place at the right time. That is a system failure, not an information gap. Option C conflates harm severity with preventability — these are independent axes. A near-miss with no harm can still be Level 3 preventable; the question is whether better process would have prevented the error, not whether injury occurred. Option D is partially correct (the prescriber bears responsibility) but misses the system-level fix: blaming an individual without fixing the transcription gap will not prevent recurrence.
debrief.rule_cited: Peer review preventability classification — NAHQ HQ Essentials: Peer Review; WHO Patient Safety Curriculum Guide Topic 5.

title: Write an operational definition — TB sputum turnaround
brief:
The PHC clinic's QI team has chosen a new process measure: **proportion of TB-suspect outpatients who receive a sputum smear microscopy result within 48 hours of sample submission**.

Before data collection begins, the team needs a written operational definition that any two nurses at this clinic could read and use to count the same way.

task.stem: Write a complete operational definition for this measure.
task.context:
**Measure:** Proportion of TB-suspect outpatients with sputum smear microscopy result within 48 hours of sample submission.

**Setting:** District-level PHC clinic. Sputum samples are logged in a paper TB laboratory register and sent to the district lab. Results are phoned back to the clinic and recorded in the same register.
task.placeholder:
Write your operational definition here. Aim to include: numerator, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, data source, and measurement window.

Example format:
Numerator: ...
Denominator: ...
Inclusions: ...
Exclusions: ...
Data source: ...
Measurement window: ...

rubric.label: Numerator — counts the desired event
rubric.hint: Should describe TB-suspect patients whose result was received AND recorded within 48 hours of sample submission.

rubric.label: Denominator — defines the eligible population
rubric.hint: Should identify all TB-suspect outpatients who submitted a sputum sample in the period — regardless of whether the result arrived in time.

rubric.label: Inclusions — explicitly names who or what is in scope
rubric.hint: e.g., includes first-episode and retreatment suspects; includes samples taken on repeat visits.

rubric.label: Exclusions — explicitly names who or what is out of scope
rubric.hint: e.g., excludes samples where the lab register shows the sample was rejected or lost in transit.

rubric.label: Data source — a named record or system
rubric.hint: Should name the specific document or system — e.g., paper TB laboratory register, DHIS2 TB module, clinic referral logbook.

debrief.correct: A strong operational definition names all six components: **numerator** (who was counted as timely), **denominator** (all eligible patients submitted), **inclusions** (who is in scope), **exclusions** (who is out of scope), **data source** (the named register or system), and **measurement window** (the review period). With all six specified, two data collectors at different clinics should reach the same count from the same register.
debrief.wrong: Check that your definition addresses all six components. The most common gaps: writing the numerator as 'patients with a result' without specifying the 48-hour cut-off; omitting exclusions entirely; naming a vague data source like 'the register' without specifying *which* register; and forgetting the measurement window. Re-read the debrief rubric and try again.
debrief.rule_cited: Operational definitions — six components: numerator, denominator, inclusions, exclusions, data source, measurement window. Provost & Murray ch. 3; IHI QI 102.

title: RCA2 — match contributing factors to causal levels
brief:
A patient at Nakuru District Hospital received the wrong blood type (B+ instead of O+) during a routine post-operative transfusion. The patient survived after emergency treatment for a haemolytic reaction.

The hospital safety committee has completed an investigation using the **RCA² framework**, which organises contributing factors into three causal levels:

- **Human factors** — the immediate actions or omissions of an individual at the point of care
- **Process factors** — the tasks, protocols, or technology that should have prevented the error
- **System / organisational factors** — the policies, training systems, and governance structures that create the conditions for error

task.stem: Match each contributing factor identified in the RCA² to the correct causal level.

items.label: The nurse checked the blood bag label only once, not twice as required.
The pre-transfusion protocol required two-nurse verification but the second nurse was not called.
The blood bank used a manual logbook with no cross-reference check against the patient wristband.
The hospital had no mandatory transfusion competency assessment for nurses newly deployed from other wards.
Ward staffing was 60% below standard on the day of the incident due to delayed salary payments.

categories.label: Human factor (individual action / omission at point of care)
Process factor (task, protocol, or technology gap)

debrief.correct: Well matched. **Human factors** are the acts or omissions of the individual at the bedside — here, the nurse's single-check. **Process factors** are the protocols and tools that should catch errors before they reach the patient — the two-nurse verification that was skipped and the blood bank's manual logbook without a cross-check. **System factors** are the upstream conditions that allowed those process gaps to exist — no mandatory competency check for newly deployed nurses and a staffing shortfall that increased workload pressure. RCA² aims to generate actions at the process and system levels, because fixing human factors alone (retraining one person) rarely prevents recurrence.
debrief.wrong: Review the three causal levels. **Human**: the immediate action of the nurse (single-label check). **Process**: the protocol that should have caught the error (two-nurse verification) and the tool that should have flagged the mismatch (blood bank logbook cross-check). **System**: the conditions upstream of the incident (no competency assessment policy, staffing deficit). A common mistake is coding 'the nurse didn't follow protocol' as a process factor — it is a human factor; the *absence of an enforced protocol* is the process factor.
debrief.rule_cited: RCA² — three causal levels: human, process, system/organisation. NPSF RCA² guide.

title: FMEA — prioritise failure modes by risk
brief:
St. Mary's Mission Hospital is conducting a **proactive Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA)** of its oral medication dispensing process. The team has identified four failure modes and rated each on three dimensions:

- **Severity (S)**: how harmful the failure is if it reaches the patient (1 = minimal, 10 = catastrophic)
- **Probability (P)**: how likely the failure is to occur (1 = rare, 10 = almost certain)
- **Detectability (D)**: how hard it is to detect before it reaches the patient (1 = easily caught, 10 = nearly impossible to detect)

**Risk Priority Number (RPN) = S × P × D.** A higher RPN means a higher priority for corrective action.

exhibit.title: FMEA — oral medication dispensing failure modes
rows: Wrong drug dispensed — look-alike / sound-alike name confusion
Patient receives double dose — incomplete shift handover
Expired medication dispensed — monthly expiry check only
Dispensing label is illegible — patient misreads dose at home

task.stem: Put the four failure modes in order from highest to lowest Risk Priority Number (RPN = S × P × D). Drag or use the arrows to reorder.

steps.label: Double dose — incomplete handover (S=7, P=4, D=7)
Illegible label — patient misreads dose (S=6, P=5, D=5)
Wrong drug — look-alike names (S=8, P=6, D=3)

debrief.correct:
Correct order by RPN:

1. **Double dose (B): RPN = 7 × 4 × 7 = 196** — high severity, moderate probability, and difficult to detect (the patient or carer may not recognise an overdose). Highest priority.
2. **Illegible label (D): RPN = 6 × 5 × 5 = 150** — moderate on all three dimensions but worrying because detection depends on the patient reading the label correctly — an unreliable last defence.
3. **Wrong drug — LASA (A): RPN = 8 × 6 × 3 = 144** — the highest severity of the four, but relatively detectable (the dispenser may notice a name mismatch if the process is followed).
4. **Expired medication (C): RPN = 5 × 2 × 8 = 80** — lowest probability and severity; the near-impossible detectability score is high but the overall product is lowest.

The key FMEA insight: high severity alone does not drive priority — probability and detectability shape the composite risk.
debrief.wrong: Calculate RPN = S × P × D for each failure mode: Wrong drug (A) = 8×6×3 = **144**; Double dose (B) = 7×4×7 = **196**; Expired medication (C) = 5×2×8 = **80**; Illegible label (D) = 6×5×5 = **150**. Order: B (196) → D (150) → A (144) → C (80). A common error is ordering by Severity alone — in FMEA, a highly severe but rarely occurring and easily detectable failure ranks lower than a moderately severe but common and hard-to-detect failure.
debrief.rule_cited: FMEA: RPN = Severity × Probability × Detectability. Higher RPN = higher priority for corrective action.

title: Just Culture — classify the behaviour
brief:
Sister Amaka is a registered nurse on a busy medical ward. The ward protocol requires **two-person identity verification** before administering any oral medication — one nurse prepares the doses, a second independently confirms the patient's name and wristband before the patient swallows the tablets.

On Tuesday morning, Sister Amaka is preparing medications when a colleague calls urgently for help with a drip. She hands the dose cup to the patient and says “Please take these tablets” without performing the second identity check. An incident report filed later shows that the patient received medication intended for the patient in the next bed. The other patient noticed the tablets looked different and did not take them — no harm resulted.

Sister Amaka tells the safety officer: “I know we’re supposed to do the two-check, but when you’ve been on this ward for three years and know every patient, it really just adds time. I skip it when we are busy.”

The **Just Culture framework** (Marx, 2001) classifies behaviours as:
- **Human error** — an inadvertent, unintended act; the person did not choose to deviate
- **At-risk behaviour** — a conscious choice to deviate from a safe practice, without recognising the risk; the person normalised the shortcut
- **Reckless behaviour** — conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk

task.stem: Using the Just Culture framework, how should Sister Amaka's behaviour be classified?

options.label: Human error — she made an inadvertent slip when distracted by the colleague's call
At-risk behaviour — she made a repeated, conscious choice to bypass a safety step she considered unnecessary, without recognising the risk
Reckless behaviour — she consciously disregarded a known and substantial risk to the patient
