task.reasonStem: What is the strongest reason for that classification?

reasons.label: The protocol violation was unintentional — she was interrupted and forgot to complete the check this one time
She routinely skipped the step because she believed it added no value, normalising a deviation without understanding the risk it created
She knew skipping the check was dangerous but chose convenience over patient safety

debrief.correct: Correct — **at-risk behaviour**. Sister Amaka's statement reveals a pattern: she skips the step routinely when busy because she perceives it as unnecessary overhead. That is not a slip (human error) — it is a habitual, conscious choice. However, it is not reckless: she does not appear to recognise that the two-check prevents a real class of errors. She has normalised the deviation. The Just Culture response to at-risk behaviour is not punishment — it is understanding why the shortcut was attractive (workload, perceived low risk) and redesigning the system so the safe path is also the easy path.
debrief.wrong: Review the three categories. **Human error** requires the deviation to be unintentional — Sister Amaka's statement ('I skip it when we are busy') confirms this is a deliberate, repeated choice, not a slip. **Reckless behaviour** requires her to consciously recognise and disregard the risk — her statement suggests she did not believe the risk was real ('when you know every patient'). That leaves **at-risk behaviour**: a conscious shortcut taken without appreciating the hazard. The Just Culture response is coaching and system redesign, not punitive action.
debrief.rule_cited: Just Culture framework — Marx (2001): human error, at-risk behaviour, reckless behaviour.

title: Safety event management — trace the reporting gap
brief:
The safety event management cycle has five stages: **(1) Detection** — recognising a near-miss or adverse event; **(2) Reporting** — submitting the incident to the designated person or system; **(3) Triage and escalation** — the safety officer classifying severity and notifying the appropriate committee; **(4) Review and learning** — the safety committee analysing the event and agreeing on corrective actions; **(5) Feedback and closure** — communicating findings and changes back to the staff who reported.

You are the newly appointed quality officer at Bwindi Community Hospital. Work through three decisions about a recent near-miss.

branches.stem: A nurse discovers she has just dispensed an amoxicillin suspension at a dose 10× higher than prescribed. She catches it before the child swallows it. What should she do FIRST in the safety event management cycle?

options.label: File an incident report to the patient safety officer before the end of her shift.
Call the prescribing doctor immediately to discuss the prescription.
Document only the final patient outcome in the clinical notes, since no harm occurred.

branches.stem: The nurse files the report. You receive it and classify it as a near-miss with potential for severe harm. Three weeks later you check the safety committee meeting minutes — the report was never discussed, because you forgot to forward it. Which stage of the reporting cycle broke down?

options.label: Detection — the nurse did not recognise the event correctly.
Triage and escalation — the safety officer (you) failed to forward the classified report to the committee.
Review and learning — the committee chose not to review this type of event.

branches.stem: You forward the report. The committee reviews it and recommends a new 'double-check before dispensing liquid doses' policy. The policy is printed and filed. Six months later the nurse who filed the original report has never heard the outcome. Which stage is now missing?

options.label: Triage — the original severity classification needs to be updated.
Review — the committee needs to reconvene and strengthen the recommendation.
Feedback and closure — the reporter and frontline staff never received the outcome, so the learning loop is incomplete.

debrief.correct: Well navigated. The reporting cycle only produces learning when all five stages complete: the near-miss is **detected** and **reported** before the end of the shift (even for no-harm events — the near-miss is data); the safety officer **triages and escalates** to the committee without delay; the committee **reviews** and agrees on corrective action; and critically, staff receive **feedback** — the learning loop closure stage. The last stage is the most commonly missed. When reporters never hear the outcome, reporting rates fall: staff conclude 'nothing changes,' so incidents go unreported.
debrief.wrong: Review the five stages: Detection → Reporting → Triage & escalation → Review & learning → Feedback & closure. Work through each branch: the first error was a failure to escalate (stage 3), not a detection or reporting failure. The final gap is stage 5 — feedback — because the nurse and her colleagues never learned what changed as a result of their report.
debrief.rule_cited: Safety event management cycle: five stages ending in feedback and learning loop closure. WHO Patient Safety Curriculum, Topic 6.

title: Swiss Cheese — latent vs active failures
brief:
James Reason's **Swiss Cheese model** explains how serious incidents occur when multiple system defences fail simultaneously. It distinguishes two types of failure:

- **Latent failures** — pre-existing weaknesses hidden within the system (the 'holes' in the cheese slices): absent policies, poor design, inadequate training, or faulty equipment. Latent failures create conditions where harm becomes possible.
- **Active failures** — the unsafe acts of individuals at the sharp end of care: slips, lapses, mistakes, or deliberate shortcuts. Active failures are the immediate trigger, but they occur because latent conditions allowed them.

**Case:** A community health worker (CHW) is conducting a contraceptive outreach day at a remote village. She administers an injectable contraceptive at twice the correct dose. The patient reports prolonged side-effects two weeks later.

task.stem: Match each factor identified in the incident review to its correct type: latent failure or active failure.

items.label: The CHW drew up the dose from memory rather than measuring against a reference card.
The supervising nurse did not visually check the prepared injection before the CHW administered it.
No dose reference card was available at the outreach site — they were kept at the base clinic.
Two concentrations of the same injectable contraceptive were stored together in one bag without separate labels.
The CHW had received no refresher training on contraceptive dosing protocols in the 18 months since her induction.

categories.label: Active failure — an immediate unsafe act by an individual at the point of care
Latent failure — a pre-existing system weakness that created the conditions for harm

debrief.correct: Correct. **Active failures** are what the individuals did in the moment: the CHW's undocumented dose draw-up and the supervisor's failure to check. These are the 'sharp end' acts that directly preceded the harm. **Latent failures** are the system gaps that made those acts more likely and removed the safety nets: no reference card at the outreach site (missing safeguard), two concentrations stored without labelling (poor physical design), and 18 months without a dosing refresher (training system gap). The Swiss Cheese insight is this: focusing only on the CHW's active failure ('she should have measured correctly') will not prevent recurrence — the latent holes will still be there for the next incident. Lasting safety improvement requires closing the latent gaps.
debrief.wrong: Review the distinction. **Active failures** are acts that the individual took (or failed to take) in real time at the moment of care — here, dosing from memory and the missed supervision check. **Latent failures** are pre-existing conditions in the system that enabled those acts — no reference card, poor storage labelling, absent refresher training. A common error is classifying 'the supervisor didn't check' as a latent failure because 'supervision is a system issue' — but the supervision step existed; the supervisor individually chose not to perform it in that moment, making it an active failure.
debrief.rule_cited: Reason's Swiss Cheese model — latent vs active failures. Reason J (1997), Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents.

title: Signal, or just noise?
brief:
Your medical ward tracks **inpatient falls per 1,000 bed-days**, monthly. This month's point ticked up to 2.0, and the {{exec}} has asked you to launch an emergency falls-prevention drive this week.

Before you act, apply the four run-chart signals to the last 14 months (median = 1.5). Then decide what to advise.

(A signal is a pattern a rule detects: a shift of six or more consecutive points on one side of the median, a trend of five or more all rising or all falling, too few or too many runs, or one astronomical point obviously different from the rest.)

exhibit.title: Inpatient falls per 1,000 bed-days (monthly)

task.stem: What do you advise the {{exec}}?

options.label: Launch the emergency falls-prevention drive this week and set a stretch target, because the rate is climbing.
Hold: no run-chart rule has fired, so this is common-cause variation. Keep the current process and keep measuring.
Remove the 2.0 point as an outlier and recompute the median so the chart looks stable.
Declare the ward unsafe and escalate the single month to the board immediately.

reasons.label: Because reacting to ordinary variation — tampering — adds new variation and can make the system worse; act only on a genuine signal, and one uptick is the two-point trap.
Because falls data is always noise and never worth acting on.
Because you need at least 24 data points before any run-chart rule can be applied.
Because the Medical Director's request outranks what the chart shows.

debrief.correct: Exactly. Run the four rules and nothing fires: the points alternate around the median (no run of six — no **shift**), there is no run of five rising or falling (no **trend**), the number of runs is ordinary (no **runs** signal), and 2.0 is only about 1.3× the median with 1.8 close behind — not an **astronomical** point. So the uptick is **common-cause noise**. Acting on it is **tampering** — the single most common data mistake in QI — and it usually makes the next month worse while burning the team's trust. The disciplined answer is: note it, keep watching, change nothing yet. (Contrast this with a true astronomical point — say a jump to 5.3 after a power failure — which *would* warrant investigating the system.)
debrief.wrong: The four signals are your bright lines. Here none of them fires: no six-in-a-row shift, no five-point trend, no runs signal, and 2.0 is not obviously different from the rest (1.8 is close, and it is only ~1.3× the median). A single worse month is the **two-point trap**. Reacting to noise is **tampering** — it injects fresh variation and exhausts staff. Only act when you can name the rule and the points that fired.
debrief.rule_cited: Common- vs special-cause variation; the four run-chart signals; the tampering trap — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104.

title: ‘Who is responsible for the bad month?’
brief:
You present a run chart of monthly **caesarean-section surgical site infection (SSI) %** to the {{board_meeting}}. A theatre-checklist change was introduced at M11, and the rate has sat below the median ever since. The {{exec}} points at M2 (one of the high early months) and asks: ‘That month is bad — **who is responsible**?’

The whole room is now looking at you.

exhibit.title: Caesarean-section SSI % (monthly) — checklist change at M11

task.stem: How do you respond to the {{exec}}?

options.label: Name the staff on duty in M2 and add the month to their performance appraisal.
Reframe: ask whether the chart is being used to improve the process or to judge the unit, then point to the sustained shift below the median since the M11 change.
Delete the pre-change months so only the good data is shown to the board.
Add a red / amber / green rating to every month so the board can grade performance at a glance.

reasons.label: Because improvement data (plotted over time, owned by the team, used to learn) and judgment data (a snapshot used to hold a unit to account) answer different questions; using an improvement chart to assign blame is a frame collision that kills learning.
Because the board owns the meeting and its accountability questions must always be answered directly.
Because one month above the median is a special-cause signal that requires naming the responsible individual.
Because run charts should never be shown in governance meetings.

debrief.correct: Well handled. This is a **frame collision**: an improvement chart pulled into a judgment conversation. Solberg's three faces of measurement — improvement, judgment/accountability, and research — answer different questions, and one number cannot serve all three at once. M2 is not a special-cause signal to pin on a person; the real story is the **shift** — ten consecutive months below the median since the M11 checklist change. The reframe (‘are we using this to improve the process or to judge the unit?’) redirects the room from blame to learning, and then you tell the improvement story.
debrief.wrong: Naming names, hiding data, or traffic-lighting the chart all deepen the **judgment frame** and destroy the learning the chart was built for. This is a **frame collision** — improvement data used to grade a unit. Solberg's three faces (improvement vs judgment vs research) are distinct purposes. Name the frame first (‘improve the process, or judge the unit?’), then point to the signal that matters: a sustained shift below the median since M11.
debrief.rule_cited: Solberg's three faces of performance measurement (improvement / judgment / research); frame collision — Solberg LI, Mosser G, McDonald S. Jt Comm J Qual Improv. 1997;23(3):135–47; NAHQ HQCF.

title: One chart, one paragraph, one decision
brief:
You are turning an improving caesarean-section SSI run chart into a one-page {{board}}. The page has one chart (the run chart, with the checklist change annotated) and one short paragraph of commentary. All that remains is the closing **decision-asked** sentence — the single line that tells leadership exactly what you want them to do.

A strong decision-ask names one action (one verb) and one time horizon.

task.stem: Which closing decision-asked sentence is strongest?

options.label: ‘The data shows encouraging progress and the team has worked very hard this quarter.’
‘We ask the {{exec}} to endorse continuing the theatre-checklist routine for the next six months, and to review it against this same chart at month 37.’
‘We should probably keep doing what we are doing and maybe look at it again at some point.’
‘We recommend endorsing the checklist, expanding it to two more theatres, hiring an audit clerk, buying a new steriliser, and revising the antibiotic policy.’

debrief.correct: Yes. The **One Chart · One Paragraph · One Decision** structure ends with a decision-asked sentence that has **one verb** (‘endorse’) and **one time horizon** (‘six months, review at month 37’). Leadership knows precisely what is being asked and cannot drift into a generic conversation. The other options fail predictably: the first states progress but asks for nothing; the third is vague with no verb or horizon; the fourth bundles five asks, so the board can approve the easy ones and quietly drop the rest.
debrief.wrong: A board one-pager exists to produce a decision. The strongest closing line names **one action and one time horizon** — ‘endorse continuing the routine for six months, review at M37.’ A sentence that only praises the team asks for nothing; a vague ‘maybe look again’ has no verb or horizon; a five-part shopping list lets the board cherry-pick. One chart, one paragraph, one decision.
debrief.rule_cited: One Chart · One Paragraph · One Decision — executive-friendly reporting; communicating data for a decision — Provost & Murray ch. 7; NAHQ HQCF (Professional Engagement).

title: Find the trend signal
brief:
Your antenatal clinic introduced a phone-reminder system to lift **ANC fourth-visit completion**. The chart shows the last 16 weeks (median = 51%).

Using Provost & Murray's **trend rule** — five or more consecutive points all going up (or all going down) signal a non-random change — click the points that make up the trend.

(Keyboard users: press Tab to enter the chart, Left/Right arrow to move between points, Enter to select.)

exhibit.title: ANC fourth-visit completion (%) — weekly

task.stem: Click each point that is part of the trend (the run of consecutive points all moving in the same direction). Submit when you have the full trend selected.

debrief.correct: Spotted. Weeks 7–12 rise every single week — 41 → 48 → 54 → 60 → 66 → 71 — that is **six** consecutive increasing points, which meets the trend rule (five or more). The run clearly *starts* at week 7 (week 6 → week 7 is a drop) and *ends* at week 12 (week 12 → week 13 falls back). Direction, not level, is the signal: it is the sustained climb that tells you the reminder system is changing the system, not any single week's value.
debrief.wrong: The trend rule: **five or more consecutive points all going up, or all going down.** Find where the line climbs without interruption — weeks 7 to 12 rise every week (41 → 48 → 54 → 60 → 66 → 71). The pre-run wobble (weeks 1–6) and the plateau after week 12 are not part of the trend. Count the *direction* of each step, not how high the points are.
debrief.rule_cited: Provost & Murray (2nd ed.) — Trend rule (≥ 5 consecutive points all increasing or all decreasing). Call it at the fifth point; do not wait for the slope to flatten.

title: Find the astronomical point
brief:
The ward tracks **medication administration errors per 1,000 doses**, monthly (median = 5). One month stands out. The rota that month leaned heavily on locum staff.

Using Provost & Murray's **astronomical-point rule** — one point that is obviously, strikingly different from all the others — click the single point that is the signal.

(Keyboard users: press Tab to enter the chart, Left/Right arrow to move between points, Enter to select.)

exhibit.title: Medication administration errors per 1,000 doses — monthly

task.stem: Click the single point that is the astronomical-point signal. Submit when it is selected.

debrief.correct: That's the one. Month 10 reads 19 per 1,000 doses against a median of 5 — nearly **four times** the usual level and far outside the ordinary month-to-month band (4–6). One point that obviously different is an **astronomical point**, and it fires on its own — you do not need a run around it. Crucially, it points you to **investigate that specific month** (the locum-heavy rota), not to conclude the whole system has deteriorated. Fix the assignable cause; don't tamper with a system that is otherwise stable.
debrief.wrong: The astronomical-point rule is the eyeball test: **one point strikingly different from all the rest.** Every month sits in a tight 4–6 band except month 10, which jumps to 19 — about four times the median of 5. That single point is the signal. It tells you to investigate *what was different that month* (here, a locum-heavy rota), not to overhaul a system that is otherwise in control.
debrief.rule_cited: Provost & Murray (2nd ed.) — Astronomical-point rule (one point obviously different from the others); investigate the special cause, do not tamper with the stable system.

title: Name the signal — hand hygiene
brief:
Your ward launched a hand-hygiene campaign after week 8. The chart shows weekly hand-hygiene compliance (%) over 16 weeks, with the median drawn as a dashed line.

Apply the four run-chart signals and name the one you see.

exhibit.title: Hand-hygiene compliance (%) — weekly

task.stem: Which run-chart signal does this chart show?

options.label: A shift — a run of six or more points on one side of the median.
A trend — five or more points all climbing or all falling.
An astronomical point — one point strikingly different from the rest.
No signal — just ordinary variation.

debrief.correct: Yes — a **shift**. From week 9 onward, eight consecutive points sit above the median (67%), well past the threshold of six. The single jump between week 8 and week 9 is not a trend (a trend needs five consecutive steps in one direction), and no point is astronomically far from the rest. A shift up in a 'good' measure like compliance is improvement — and it is holding.
debrief.wrong: Count the points on one side of the median. From week 9, eight weeks in a row sit above the median (67%) — that is a **shift** (six or more consecutive on one side). It is not a trend (no run of five consecutive *steps* up or down) and there is no single astronomical outlier.
debrief.rule_cited: Shift rule — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104.

title: Name the signal — or is there one?
brief:
A manager glances at this chart of weekly antenatal-clinic attendance (%) and wants to 'do something about the dips'. The median is the dashed line.

Apply the four run-chart signals before you answer — and be honest if none of them fires.

exhibit.title: Antenatal-clinic attendance (%) — weekly

task.stem: Which run-chart signal does this chart show?

options.label: A shift — a run of six or more points on one side of the median.
A trend — five or more points all climbing or all falling.
An astronomical point — one point strikingly different from the rest.
No signal — this is ordinary (common-cause) variation.

debrief.correct: Correct — **no signal**. The points wobble either side of the median (70%) with no run of six on one side (no shift), no run of five consecutive steps in one direction (no trend), and no point strikingly far from the rest (no astronomical point). This is ordinary **common-cause variation**. Acting on the 'dips' would be **tampering** — reacting to noise. The disciplined response is to keep watching and change nothing yet.
debrief.wrong: Check each rule. Longest run on one side of the median is only two (no shift); the longest string of consecutive up-or-down steps is short (no trend); no point is dramatically different (no astronomical point). So **no signal fires** — this is common-cause noise. Reacting to it would be tampering. Keep watching; change nothing yet.
debrief.rule_cited: Common- vs special-cause variation; the tampering trap — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104.

title: Find the trend — laboratory turnaround
brief:
The laboratory started a new sample-transport run to cut **turnaround time** (minutes; lower is better). The chart shows 14 weeks, median dashed.

Using the **trend rule** — five or more consecutive points all moving in the same direction — click the points that make up the trend.

(Keyboard users: Tab into the chart, arrow keys to move, Enter to select.)

exhibit.title: Laboratory turnaround time (minutes) — weekly

task.stem: Click each point that is part of the trend (the run of consecutive points all moving the same way). Submit when you have the full trend selected.

debrief.correct: Spotted. Weeks 5–10 fall every single week — 175 → 160 → 148 → 135 → 120 → 108 — that is **six** consecutive decreasing points, which meets the trend rule (five or more). The run clearly starts at week 5 (week 4 → week 5 drops after a rise) and ends at week 10 (the line flattens after). A falling trend in turnaround time is improvement.
debrief.wrong: The trend rule: **five or more consecutive points all moving one way.** Find the unbroken descent — weeks 5 to 10 fall every week (175 → 160 → 148 → 135 → 120 → 108). The early wobble (weeks 1–4) and the plateau after week 10 are not part of the trend. Judge the *direction* of each step, not the height of the points.
debrief.rule_cited: Trend rule — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104. Call it at the fifth consecutive step; do not wait for the slope to flatten.

title: A signal in the wrong direction
brief:
This chart shows the monthly **catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) rate** per 1,000 catheter-days (lower is better). The median is the dashed line.

A colleague says: 'Six months in a row above the line — at least it's consistent.' Read the chart and decide what it really means.

exhibit.title: CAUTI rate per 1,000 catheter-days — monthly

task.stem: What does this pattern tell you?

options.label: Good news — the rate is stable and consistent; no action needed.
A real signal in the undesirable direction — a sustained upward shift. Investigate what changed around M9 and act.
Just noise — every month varies; ignore it.
An improvement — six months in a row is a good run.

reasons.label: A run of six or more points on one side of the median is a shift — and direction matters. Here the shift is upward on a 'lower-is-better' measure, so it demands investigation and action, not reassurance.
Any movement on a chart means the process is out of control and must be stopped.
An upward run is always a good sign.
You must always wait for at least 24 points before reading any signal.

debrief.correct: Exactly. From M9, eight consecutive months sit **above** the median (3.0) — a clear **shift**. A shift is a real special-cause signal, but **direction matters**: on a lower-is-better measure like CAUTI, an upward shift is a deterioration, not a 'consistent' or 'good' run. The right move is to investigate what changed around M9 (a new catheter practice? a staffing change? a supply switch?) and act. Reading the direction wrong is how teams celebrate a signal that should alarm them.
debrief.wrong: Two things to get right. First, this **is** a signal: eight months in a row above the median is a shift (six or more on one side). Second, and just as important, the **direction**: CAUTI is a lower-is-better measure, so an upward shift is a worsening. It is neither noise to ignore nor good news to celebrate — investigate what changed around M9 and act.
debrief.rule_cited: Shift rule and the importance of direction — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104.

title: Is this even enough data?
brief:
A team has plotted its first **six weeks** of theatre start-time delays (minutes) and is keen to declare that things are improving. The median is the dashed line.

Before reading any signal, ask the prior question: is there enough data?

exhibit.title: Theatre start-time delay (minutes) — weekly

task.stem: Can you reliably apply the run-chart rules to this chart yet?

options.label: Yes — six points is plenty to call a signal.
No — you generally need about 10–12 points or more before the rules are reliable; keep collecting.
Yes, but only the astronomical-point rule works with few points.
No — you need exactly 30 points before any run chart can be read.

debrief.correct: Right. With only six points, the run-chart rules are not yet reliable — you generally want **about 10–12 points or more** before a shift, trend, or runs signal means much. Six points can look like an improvement purely by chance. Keep collecting data on the same measure, keep the median provisional, and re-read the chart as it grows. Declaring victory now risks acting on noise.
debrief.wrong: The run-chart rules need enough data to work: **roughly 10–12 points or more**. Six points is too few — a short downward wiggle can happen by chance and is not a signal. It is not that only one rule works, and there is no magic '30 points' threshold; you simply keep collecting until the chart is long enough to read.
debrief.rule_cited: Minimum data for run-chart interpretation — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.); Perla, Provost & Murray on run-chart rules.

title: The runs rule — the technical fourth check
brief:
Three of the four run-chart signals are easy to eyeball: a shift (six on one side), a trend (five in one direction), and an astronomical point (one obvious outlier). The fourth — the **runs** rule — is more technical.

A 'run' is a set of consecutive points on the same side of the median. You count how many runs the chart has and compare that number to a lookup table for that many data points.

task.stem: A chart has far FEWER runs (fewer crossings of the median) than the lookup table expects for its number of points. What does that suggest?

options.label: Nothing — the number of runs is never meaningful.
A non-random signal — too few runs means the data is clustering on one side; check the count against the runs lookup table.
The median must have been calculated incorrectly.
You should immediately add control limits to the chart.

debrief.correct: Yes. **Too few runs** (the line rarely crosses the median) or **too many runs** (it crosses far more often than chance) both signal non-random behaviour. Unlike the eyeball rules, the runs rule is judged against a **lookup table**: for a given number of points, the table gives the expected minimum and maximum number of runs, and falling outside that range is the signal. It is the 'technical fourth check' — reach for the table when the other three rules are quiet but the pattern still looks off. You do not need to memorise the table; you need to know it exists and how to use it.
debrief.wrong: The runs rule counts how many times the line crosses the median. **Too few or too many runs** — compared with a lookup table for that number of points — is a non-random signal. It is a real rule (the number of runs is meaningful), it is not about a mis-calculated median, and it does not require control limits (those belong to SPC / Part 2). Use the lookup table; you don't have to memorise it.
debrief.rule_cited: Runs rule (number of runs vs the runs lookup table) — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104.

title: Points that land on the median
brief:
You are counting a run for the shift rule (six or more consecutive points on one side of the median). As you count along, you reach a point whose value is **exactly equal to the median**.

How should you treat it?

task.stem: How do you treat a point that lands exactly on the median when counting a shift?

options.label: Count it as above the median.
Count it as below the median.
Skip it — points on the median don't count toward the run, and they don't reset it.
Start the count over from that point.

debrief.correct: Correct. A point sitting **exactly on the median** is neither above nor below, so you **skip it** — it does not add to the run, and it does not break or reset it. You simply carry on counting the points either side. Treating on-median points as above or below (or restarting the count) is a common way people miscount a shift.
debrief.wrong: A point exactly on the median is neither above nor below it, so it can't count toward a run on either side. The convention is to **skip it** — it doesn't add to the run and doesn't reset it; you keep counting the points that are clearly above or below. This is why the median (not the mean) is used and why 'points on the line' need a rule of their own.
debrief.rule_cited: Counting runs and shifts — points on the median are excluded — Provost & Murray (2nd ed.), IHI QI 104.

title: Read the whole fishbone
brief: A ward team is reviewing repeated delays in giving the first antibiotic dose for suspected sepsis. The fishbone groups possible contributors instead of blaming the last person in the chain.

exhibit.title: Possible causes of delayed first antibiotic dose

task.stem: What is the best next use of this fishbone?

options.label: Choose the person named most often and retrain them.
Verify the leading hypotheses with observations and data before selecting changes.
Treat every listed cause as proven and launch all changes at once.
Calculate a control limit for each branch.

debrief.correct: Correct. A fishbone organizes hypotheses; it does not prove causation. Verify the strongest process and system hypotheses before choosing a focused test of change.
debrief.wrong: The branches contain hypotheses, not verdicts. Use observation, record review, and small tests to learn which contributors actually drive the delay.
debrief.rule_cited: Systems-based cause analysis — hypotheses require verification before action.

title: Tell the I-chart story honestly
brief: The {{exec}} asks whether a single unusually long discharge time proves that the entire process has deteriorated. Use the I-chart to answer and defend the recommendation.

exhibit.title: Weekly median discharge time in hours

task.stem: What should you advise?

options.label: Investigate W6 as a possible special cause without claiming the whole process shifted.
Announce that the process average has permanently worsened.
Ignore W6 because one point can never matter.

reasons.label: A point beyond the limits merits investigation, while the surrounding series does not show a sustained shift.
The target line is the same as a control limit.
Only monthly data can show special causes.

debrief.correct: Correct. Investigate the exceptional week, describe it as a possible special cause, and avoid overstating a permanent system change.
debrief.wrong: One exceptional point can deserve investigation without supporting a claim that the whole process permanently shifted.
debrief.rule_cited: Control-chart interpretation — distinguish an isolated special cause from a sustained change.

title: Turn an equity gap into a testable action
brief: Follow-up after hypertension referral is high near the district centre and much lower in remote catchment areas. The {{exec2}} wants one practical next step.

exhibit.title: Referral follow-up completed within 30 days

items.label: District centre
Peri-urban
Remote north
Remote river

task.stem: Which action should you recommend first?

options.label: Test transport-linked appointment days in one remote catchment and measure completion plus missed visits.
Publish the district average and avoid subgroup targets.
Move all appointments to the district centre.

task.reasonStem: Why is that the strongest first step?

reasons.label: It targets the observed access mechanism, starts small, and includes outcome and balancing evidence.
Every geographic gap is caused only by transport.
Equity work does not need measurement after implementation.

debrief.correct: Correct. The test is targeted, small enough to learn from, and measures both follow-up and unintended burden.
debrief.wrong: A useful equity response connects the observed gap to a plausible access mechanism, tests one change, and measures whether the gap improves without creating new burden.
debrief.rule_cited: Equity-stratified improvement — act on a plausible mechanism and measure the result.
